summary: Describes an on-line hostnames service, part of the discussion with RFCs 606, 608, 623 and 627.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 625 agrees that the host-name database should have secondary copies but argues against a dedicated server process. Its authors prefer using FTP to transfer the sequential ASCII file because it is easier to inspect and troubleshoot.

subtitle: A response supporting FTP and ASCII for distributing host names.

tldr.problem: The authors respond to proposals about secondary host-name database copies, a dedicated server process and a binary database format.
tldr.mechanism: They support the NIC maintaining the master file and welcoming secondary copies, but argue that FTP suits retrieval of the sequential file and ASCII makes it easier to inspect and troubleshoot.
tldr.outcome: The RFC records the NIC authors' disagreement with some suggestions in RFC 623; it does not announce a new protocol.

today: RFC 625 records the NIC authors' response to design suggestions for distributing the host-name database.

sections.title: Agreement on Secondary Copies
sections.content: The authors agree with RFC 623 that more than one host should maintain a copy of the host-name database. The NIC is willing to keep the master database and make it available to secondary hosts that volunteer; the authors welcome UCSB as one such host.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors support keeping secondary copies of the database. The NIC would continue to maintain the master and make it available to volunteers.

sections.title: FTP Rather Than a Dedicated Server
sections.content:
The authors disagree with the suggestion to create a server process for access to the NIC's official host-name file. Because the file is sequential, they consider FTP appropriate for retrieving it. They also say agreeing on common login parameters does not seem like a major problem, and that a dedicated process would still require additional protocol agreements.

They argue that FTP was intended as a reusable network file-transfer mechanism and suggest that criticism should lead to improving or replacing FTP rather than bypassing it for each simple application.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors think FTP is a reasonable way to transfer this sequential file. They say a separate service would still need rules for how programs use it.

sections.title: Preference for ASCII
sections.content: The authors also prefer to keep the host-name file in ASCII rather than binary. They say ASCII makes it easier to check the data and diagnose transfer problems.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors prefer a text file because people can inspect it when checking the data or investigating a transfer problem.
